nodes.label: Tornado
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: A violent rotating column of air extending from a thunderstorm to the ground. Tornadoes are smaller but more intense than cyclones. They can cause extreme damage in narrow paths. Most common in the USA. Wind speeds can exceed 300 km/h.

nodes.label: Biodiversity
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Term popularised by sociobiologist Edward Wilson to describe combined diversity at all levels of biological organisation. Over 1.5 million species described so far (IUCN 2004). Robert May estimates global species diversity at ~7 million. Over 70% of recorded species are animals; insects make up >70% of all animals. Fungi species exceed combined total of fishes, amphibians, reptiles, and mammals. India has 2.4% of world's land area but 8.1% of global species diversity, making it one of 12 mega diversity countries.

nodes.label: Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD)
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Historic convention held at Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro, 1992. Called upon all nations to take appropriate measures for conservation of biodiversity and sustainable utilisation of its benefits. Follow-up: World Summit on Sustainable Development in Johannesburg, 2002 - 190 countries pledged to achieve significant reduction in biodiversity loss by 2010. Biodiversity knows no political boundaries; conservation is collective responsibility of all nations.

nodes.label: Solar Energy
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Energy from the Sun, which has been radiating for ~5 billion years and will continue for ~5 billion more. Solar devices: solar cookers (use mirrors to focus rays, glass plate for greenhouse effect), solar water heaters (black surfaces absorb more heat), and solar cells (convert solar energy to electricity, 0.5-1V per cell, ~0.7W output). Solar cells use silicon, have no moving parts, need little maintenance. Used in satellites, remote area power, traffic signals, calculators.

nodes.label: Wind Energy
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Kinetic energy of wind used to generate electricity via windmills driving turbines. Wind energy farms cluster many windmills for commercial-scale output. Largest wind farm in India near Kanyakumari, Tamil Nadu (380 MW). India ranked 5th globally in wind energy; Denmark generates 25%+ electricity from wind. Limitations: needs wind speed >15 km/h, requires large land area (2 hectares per 1 MW), high initial cost, high maintenance, needs backup storage.

nodes.label: Asexual Reproduction
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Reproduction from a single parent without fusion of gametes. Produces offspring genetically similar to parent. Types: fission (binary in Amoeba, multiple in Plasmodium), budding (Hydra, yeast), fragmentation (Spirogyra), regeneration (Hydra, Planaria), vegetative propagation (from roots, stems, leaves), and spore formation (Rhizopus). Faster than sexual reproduction but generates less variation.

nodes.label: Binary and Multiple Fission
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Binary fission: unicellular organism splits into two equal halves. In Amoeba, splitting can occur in any plane. In Leishmania (causes kala-azar), fission occurs in a definite orientation relative to the whip-like structure. Multiple fission: organism divides into many daughter cells simultaneously, as seen in Plasmodium (malarial parasite). Fission is the simplest mode of reproduction for unicellular organisms.

nodes.label: Vegetative Propagation
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: New plants grow from vegetative parts (roots, stems, leaves) without seeds. Used in agriculture through layering and grafting for sugarcane, roses, grapes. Advantages: plants bear flowers/fruits earlier than seed-grown ones, enables propagation of seedless plants (banana, orange, jasmine), offspring genetically identical to parent. Examples: potato (eyes/buds), Bryophyllum (buds on leaf margins), money plant (stem cuttings).

nodes.label: Sexual Reproduction
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Involves fusion of male and female gametes from two parents, producing offspring with genetic material from both. Generates greater variation than asexual reproduction, which is advantageous for species survival in changing environments. Requires energy investment for producing gametes and finding mates. Involves: germ cell formation, fertilisation, embryo development. Found in both plants and animals.

nodes.label: Reproduction in Flowering Plants
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Flower is the reproductive organ. Male part: stamen (anther produces pollen grains containing male gametes, filament supports anther). Female part: pistil/carpel (stigma receives pollen, style connects to ovary, ovary contains ovules with female gametes). Pollination: transfer of pollen from anther to stigma (self or cross). Fertilisation: pollen tube grows down style, male gamete fuses with egg in ovule. Zygote develops into embryo, ovule becomes seed, ovary becomes fruit.

nodes.label: Human Male Reproductive System
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Testes (located in scrotum outside body -- lower temperature needed for sperm formation) produce sperms and testosterone. Testosterone regulates sperm formation and puberty changes. Sperms travel through vas deferens, combine with secretions from prostate gland and seminal vesicles (provide nutrition and ease transport), and exit through urethra (common passage for sperms and urine). Sperms are tiny with genetic material and a long tail for motility.

nodes.label: Human Female Reproductive System
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Ovaries produce eggs and hormones (oestrogen). One egg matures and releases each month. Egg travels through fallopian tube (oviduct) where fertilisation occurs. Fertilised egg (zygote) divides to form embryo, implants in thickened uterine lining. Placenta (disc embedded in uterine wall with villi) provides large surface area for nutrient/oxygen transfer from mother's blood and waste removal. Gestation: approximately 9 months. Birth: rhythmic uterine contractions.

nodes.label: Menstrual Cycle
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Monthly cycle in human females. Uterine lining thickens each month to prepare for possible embryo implantation. If egg is not fertilised (it lives only about one day), the thickened lining breaks down and exits as blood and mucous through the vagina. This is menstruation, lasting 2-8 days. The cycle repeats roughly every month. Begins at puberty as a sign of sexual maturation.

nodes.label: Contraceptive Methods
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Methods to prevent pregnancy. Mechanical barriers: condoms (also prevent STDs to some extent), diaphragms. Hormonal: oral contraceptive pills change hormonal balance to prevent egg release (can have side effects). Intrauterine devices: copper-T, loop placed in uterus (can cause irritation). Surgical: vasectomy (blocking vas deferens in males), tubectomy (blocking fallopian tubes in females). Prenatal sex determination is prohibited by law to prevent female foeticide.

nodes.label: Regeneration
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Ability of some organisms to regrow complete individuals from body parts. Hydra and Planaria can be cut into many pieces, each growing into a complete organism. Carried out by specialised cells that proliferate, then differentiate into various cell types in an organised sequence (development). Regeneration is not the same as reproduction -- organisms do not normally depend on being cut up to reproduce. It demonstrates cellular totipotency.

nodes.label: Artificial Selection
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Human-directed selection of desirable traits in organisms over generations. Classic example: wild cabbage was selectively bred over 2000+ years to produce cabbage (short leaf distances), broccoli (arrested flower development), cauliflower (sterile flowers), kohlrabi (swollen parts), and kale (larger leaves). Demonstrates how selection pressure shapes diverse forms from a common ancestor.

nodes.label: Conventional Sources of Energy
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Traditional energy sources that have been in use for a long time. Include fossil fuels (coal, petroleum, natural gas), thermal power plants, and hydroelectric power. India relies heavily on fossil fuels for energy needs. These are being gradually supplemented by non-conventional sources due to depletion and environmental concerns.

nodes.label: Fossil Fuels
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Coal, petroleum, and natural gas formed from degraded biomass millions of years ago. Non-renewable and exhaustible. Burning produces oxides of carbon, nitrogen, and sulphur leading to acid rain, and CO2 causing greenhouse effect. Estimated reserves: petroleum for about 40 years, coal for about 200 years at present usage rates. Coal used in thermal power stations; petroleum products (petrol, diesel) in transport.

nodes.label: Thermal Power Plant
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Burns fossil fuels to heat water, producing steam that drives turbines to generate electricity. Located near coal or oil fields since transmitting electricity is more efficient than transporting coal/petroleum. The term 'thermal' refers to using heat energy from fuel combustion to produce electrical energy. Major contributor to India's electricity generation.

nodes.label: Hydroelectric Power
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Converts potential energy of water stored at height in dams into electricity via turbines. Renewable source meeting about 25% of India's energy needs. Problems with large dams: limited suitable locations (preferably hilly terrain), submersion of agricultural land and habitations, destruction of ecosystems, methane production from rotting submerged vegetation (greenhouse gas), displacement of people. Tehri Dam (Ganga) and Sardar Sarovar (Narmada) faced major opposition.

nodes.label: Biomass Energy
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Energy from plant and animal products: wood, cow-dung cakes, crop residue. Bio-gas (gobar-gas) is produced by anaerobic decomposition of cow-dung and plant waste in a sealed digester. Contains up to 75% methane, burns without smoke, no ash residue, high heating capacity, also used for lighting. The slurry left behind is excellent manure rich in nitrogen and phosphorus. Charcoal is made by burning wood in limited oxygen supply.

nodes.label: Ocean Thermal Energy
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Exploits temperature difference between warm surface water (heated by Sun) and cold deep water (up to 2 km depth). Requires minimum 20 K (20 degrees C) temperature difference to operate. Warm surface water boils a volatile liquid (like ammonia) whose vapours run a turbine; cold deep water pumped up to condense the vapour. OTEC plants have large potential but difficult commercial exploitation.

nodes.label: Renewable vs Non-renewable Energy
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Non-renewable (exhaustible) sources like fossil fuels and nuclear fuel will deplete over time. Renewable (inexhaustible) sources like solar, wind, hydro, and biomass can be regenerated or are practically limitless. Energy source selection depends on ease and cost of extraction, technology efficiency, and environmental impact. No source is truly pollution-free; even 'clean' sources like solar cells cause environmental damage during manufacturing.

nodes.label: Ecosystem
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: A functional unit comprising all interacting organisms in an area together with non-living components. Consists of biotic components (living organisms) and abiotic components (temperature, rainfall, wind, soil, minerals). Natural ecosystems: forests, ponds, lakes. Human-made (artificial) ecosystems: gardens, crop-fields, aquariums. All components are interdependent.

nodes.label: Producers
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Organisms that produce food through photosynthesis using solar energy, CO2, and chlorophyll. Include all green plants and certain bacteria (cyanobacteria). They form the first trophic level in any food chain. In terrestrial ecosystems, green plants capture only about 1% of sunlight energy that falls on their leaves and convert it into food energy.

nodes.label: Consumers
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Organisms that consume food produced by others. Categories: herbivores (primary consumers, eat producers directly), carnivores (secondary consumers eat herbivores; tertiary consumers eat secondary consumers), omnivores (eat both plants and animals), and parasites. Humans occupy the top level in most food chains.

nodes.label: Decomposers
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Microorganisms (bacteria and fungi) that break down dead remains and waste products of organisms into simple inorganic substances. These substances return to the soil and are used again by plants. Without decomposers, natural replenishment of soil nutrients would not occur and dead organic matter would accumulate indefinitely.

nodes.label: Food Chain
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: A series of organisms in which each member feeds on the one below it. Example: Grass -> Deer -> Lion. Each step forms a trophic level. Generally limited to 3-4 steps because energy loss at each level is so great that very little usable energy remains after four trophic levels. The number of individuals is generally greatest at the lowest trophic levels (producers).

nodes.label: Food Web
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: An interconnected network of food chains in an ecosystem. Each organism may be part of multiple food chains. Food webs show complex feeding relationships. If one species is removed, it can affect many others in the web.

nodes.label: Trophic Levels
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Each step in a food chain forms a trophic level. First trophic level: autotrophs/producers (fix solar energy). Second: herbivores/primary consumers. Third: small carnivores/secondary consumers. Fourth: larger carnivores/tertiary consumers. Energy and biomass decrease progressively from lower to higher trophic levels. Greater number of individuals typically found at lower trophic levels.

nodes.label: 10% Energy Transfer Rule
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: On average, only 10% of the food energy consumed at one trophic level is converted into biomass available for the next level. The remaining 90% is lost as heat, used in digestion, and expended in life processes. This is why food chains rarely exceed 3-4 trophic levels. The flow of energy is unidirectional -- energy captured by autotrophs never reverts to solar input, and energy at each level does not return to the previous level.

nodes.label: Biological Magnification
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The progressive accumulation of non-degradable chemicals (like pesticides) at each successive trophic level in a food chain. Pesticides and chemicals washed into soil or water are absorbed by plants or aquatic organisms and enter the food chain. Since these chemicals are not degradable, their concentration increases at higher trophic levels. Humans, at the top of most food chains, accumulate the maximum concentration. This is why food grains, vegetables, fruits, and meat contain pesticide residues.

nodes.label: Biodegradable Substances
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Substances that can be broken down by biological processes (bacteria, fungi, and other saprophytes). Include kitchen waste, vegetable peels, paper, cloth, and organic matter. These decompose naturally over time and return nutrients to the soil. Enzymes are specific in their action -- each enzyme breaks down particular substances, which is why not all materials are biodegradable.

nodes.label: Non-biodegradable Substances
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Substances not broken down by biological processes, such as plastics, glass, metals, and many synthetic chemicals. May be inert and persist in the environment for very long periods, or may actively harm ecosystem members. Human lifestyle changes and disposable culture have greatly increased non-biodegradable waste generation. Changes in packaging have made much of our waste non-biodegradable.

nodes.label: Energy Flow in Ecosystem
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Energy flow is unidirectional in an ecosystem: Sun -> producers -> primary consumers -> secondary consumers -> tertiary consumers. At each trophic level, energy is progressively diminished due to heat loss and metabolic activities. Autotrophs capture about 1% of incident solar energy and make it available for consumers. Decomposers obtain energy from dead organic matter at all levels.

nodes.label: Five Rs (Refuse, Reduce, Reuse, Repurpose, Recycle)
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Five strategies to reduce environmental pressure. Refuse: say no to unnecessary products, especially single-use plastics. Reduce: save electricity, water, don't waste food. Reuse: use items again (e.g., reverse envelopes, reuse plastic bottles). Repurpose: when original purpose is done, find new use (e.g., cracked cups as planters). Recycle: collect and process plastic, paper, glass, metal into new products. Requires waste segregation.

nodes.label: Dam Controversies
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Large dams face three categories of criticism: (1) Social: displacing large numbers of peasants and tribals without adequate compensation (e.g., Tawa Dam oustees still fighting since 1970s), (2) Economic: swallowing huge public money without proportionate benefits, inequitable water distribution, (3) Environmental: causing deforestation and loss of biological diversity. Narmada Bachao Andolan protested Sardar Sarovar Dam on Narmada. Indira Gandhi Canal brought greenery to Rajasthan but with mismanagement issues.

nodes.label: Water Harvesting
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Age-old concept in India with diverse regional practices: khadins, tanks, nadis (Rajasthan), bandharas and tals (Maharashtra), bundhis (MP and UP), ahars and pynes (Bihar), kulhs (Himachal Pradesh), ponds (Jammu Kandi belt), eris (Tamil Nadu), surangams (Kerala), kattas (Karnataka). Main purpose: recharge groundwater rather than hold surface water. Advantages of underground storage: no evaporation, wider moisture spread, no mosquito breeding, protected from contamination. Dr. Rajendra Singh built 8,600 johads in Rajasthan (won 2015 Stockholm Water Prize).

nodes.label: Kulhs of Himachal Pradesh
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Local canal irrigation system evolved over 400 years ago in Himachal Pradesh. Stream water diverted into man-made channels taking water to villages down hillsides. Management by common agreement: during planting season, the farthest village from the source used water first, then progressively closer villages. Maintained by 2-3 people paid by villagers. Water also percolated to recharge springs. After Irrigation Department took over, most kulhs became defunct.

nodes.label: Coal and Petroleum Management
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Fossil fuels formed from biomass degradation millions of years ago. Petroleum reserves estimated for about 40 years; coal for about 200 years at present usage. Burning produces CO2 (greenhouse gas), oxides of nitrogen and sulphur (poisonous, cause acid rain), and CO (from incomplete combustion). Large-scale conversion to CO2 would intensify global warming. Need for efficient internal combustion engines. Euro norms regulate vehicle emissions to reduce air pollution.

nodes.label: Watershed Management
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Emphasises scientific soil and water conservation to increase biomass production. Develops primary resources (land and water) and secondary resources (plants and animals) sustainably. Mitigates droughts and floods, increases life of downstream dams and reservoirs. Various organisations rejuvenate ancient water harvesting systems as alternatives to mega-projects. Communities use indigenous methods: small pits, lakes, simple watershed systems, earthen dams, dykes, rooftop water collection.

nodes.label: External and Internal Fertilisation
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: External fertilisation occurs outside the body in aquatic organisms (algae, fishes, amphibians) requiring synchrony and large gamete numbers. Internal fertilisation occurs inside the body in fungi, reptiles, birds, mammals, and most plants. In seed plants, non-motile male gametes are carried by pollen tubes. Parthenogenesis (development without fertilisation) occurs in some organisms like honeybees, rotifers, and turkeys.

nodes.label: Oviparous and Viviparous Animals
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Oviparous animals (reptiles, birds) lay fertilised eggs with hard calcareous shells externally; young hatch after incubation. Viviparous animals (most mammals including humans) develop the zygote inside the female body, providing better embryonic care and higher survival rates. In flowering plants, the zygote forms inside the ovule; ovule becomes seed, ovary becomes fruit with protective pericarp.

nodes.label: Monoecious and Dioecious Plants
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Monoecious (homothallic) plants bear both male and female flowers on the same individual (e.g., cucurbits, coconut). Dioecious (heterothallic) plants bear male and female flowers on separate individuals (e.g., papaya, date palm). In animals, bisexual organisms (hermaphrodites) like earthworm, sponge, and tapeworm possess both reproductive organs. Cockroach is a unisexual species.

nodes.label: Embryogenesis
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Development of embryo from zygote through cell division (mitosis) and cell differentiation. The zygote is the vital link ensuring species continuity between generations. In flowering plants, after fertilisation, sepals/petals/stamens wither; ovules develop into seeds and ovary into fruit. In organisms with haplontic life cycle, zygote divides by meiosis to form haploid spores.

nodes.label: Population Explosion in India
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: World population grew from 2 billion (1900) to about 6 billion (2000) and 7.2 billion (2011). India's population was ~350 million at independence, reached close to 1 billion by 2000, and crossed 1.2 billion in May 2011. Causes: rapid decline in death rate, maternal mortality rate (MMR), and infant mortality rate (IMR); increase in reproductive age population. 2011 census: growth rate less than 2% (20/1000/year). Measures include statutory marriageable age (18 for females, 21 for males) and incentives for small families.

nodes.label: Natural/Traditional Contraceptive Methods
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Methods avoiding ovum-sperm meeting without medicines or devices. Periodic abstinence: avoiding coitus during fertile period (days 10-17 of menstrual cycle). Coitus interruptus (withdrawal): male withdraws before ejaculation. Lactational amenorrhea: absence of menstruation during intense lactation following parturition, effective only up to 6 months post-delivery. Advantages: no side effects. Disadvantage: high failure rate.

nodes.label: Barrier Contraceptive Methods
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Physical barriers preventing ovum-sperm contact. Condoms (male - 'Nirodh' brand; female) made of thin rubber/latex, also protect against STIs and AIDS. Diaphragms, cervical caps, and vaults are rubber barriers inserted into female reproductive tract to cover cervix. Spermicidal creams, jellies, and foams used alongside barriers to increase efficiency. Condoms are disposable and self-inserted; diaphragms are reusable.

nodes.label: Intra Uterine Devices (IUDs)
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Devices inserted into uterus by doctors/nurses. Three types: non-medicated (Lippes loop), copper-releasing (CuT, Cu7, Multiload 375), and hormone-releasing (Progestasert, LNG-20). IUDs increase phagocytosis of sperms; copper ions suppress sperm motility and fertilising capacity. Hormone-releasing IUDs make uterus unsuitable for implantation and cervix hostile to sperms. One of the most widely accepted contraceptive methods in India. Ideal for spacing children.

nodes.label: Oral Contraceptive Pills
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Small doses of progestogens or progestogen-estrogen combinations taken as tablets for 21 days per cycle. They inhibit ovulation and implantation, and alter cervical mucus quality. Saheli, developed by CDRI Lucknow, is a non-steroidal oral contraceptive taken once a week with fewer side effects. Progestogens can also be administered as injectables or subcutaneous implants with longer effective periods. Emergency contraceptives (within 72 hours of coitus) include progestogens, progestogen-estrogen combinations, or IUDs.

nodes.label: Surgical Methods of Contraception
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Terminal methods blocking gamete transport. Vasectomy (male): small part of vas deferens removed or tied through scrotal incision. Tubectomy (female): small part of fallopian tube removed or tied through abdominal incision or vagina. Highly effective but reversibility is very poor. Generally advised as permanent method when no more pregnancies desired. These block gamete transport, not gamete formation.

nodes.label: Medical Termination of Pregnancy (MTP)
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Intentional/voluntary termination of pregnancy before full term. About 45-50 million MTPs performed annually worldwide (1/5th of all pregnancies). Legalised in India in 1971 with strict conditions. MTP Amendment Act 2017: allowed up to 12 weeks on one doctor's opinion, up to 24 weeks on two doctors' opinions. Safe in first trimester (up to 12 weeks); riskier in second trimester. Amniocentesis for sex determination is banned to prevent female foeticide.

nodes.label: Amniocentesis
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: A procedure where amniotic fluid of the developing foetus is extracted to analyse fetal cells and dissolved substances. Legitimate use: testing for genetic disorders like Down syndrome, haemophilia, sickle-cell anaemia, and determining foetus survivability. Misuse: sex determination of unborn child, often followed by female foeticide. Statutory ban on amniocentesis for sex determination in India to combat female foeticide.

nodes.label: Human Genome Project (HGP)
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Mega project launched in 1990, completed in 2003. Coordinated by US Department of Energy and NIH, with Wellcome Trust (UK), Japan, France, Germany, China. Goals: identify all ~20,000-25,000 human genes, determine sequence of 3 billion bp, store in databases, address ethical/legal/social issues (ELSI). Used BAC (bacterial artificial chromosomes) and YAC (yeast artificial chromosomes) as vectors. Sanger's method for sequencing. Led to development of Bioinformatics. Associated with HGP was sequencing of model organisms like E. coli, yeast, Drosophila, rice, Arabidopsis.

nodes.label: Human Genome Project - Key Findings
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Human genome: 3164.7 million bp. Average gene: 3000 bases; largest known gene: dystrophin (2.4 million bases). Total estimated genes: ~30,000 (much lower than earlier estimates of 80,000-140,000). 99.9% nucleotide bases identical across all humans. Less than 2% of genome codes for proteins. Functions unknown for over 50% of discovered genes. Chromosome 1 has most genes (2968), Y chromosome has fewest (231). About 1.4 million SNPs (single nucleotide polymorphisms) identified. Repetitive sequences form large portion of genome.

nodes.label: Oparin-Haldane Hypothesis
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Oparin (Russia) and Haldane (England) proposed that first life forms arose from pre-existing non-living organic molecules (RNA, protein). Chemical evolution preceded biological evolution: diverse organic molecules formed from inorganic constituents under conditions of high temperature, volcanic storms, and reducing atmosphere (CH4, NH3). First non-cellular forms originated ~3 billion years ago as giant molecules (RNA, protein, polysaccharides) that could reproduce.

nodes.label: Biofortification
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Breeding crops with higher levels of vitamins, minerals, protein, and healthier fats to improve public health. Objectives: improved protein content/quality, oil content/quality, vitamin content, micronutrient/mineral content. Maize hybrids with 2x lysine and tryptophan developed in 2000. Atlas 66 wheat has high protein. Iron-fortified rice with 5x iron content. IARI released vitamin A enriched carrots/spinach/pumpkin, vitamin C enriched bitter gourd/mustard/tomato, iron/calcium enriched spinach/bathua, protein enriched beans.
nodes.chapter_title: Strategies for Enhancement in Food Production

nodes.label: Single Cell Protein (SCP)
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Alternative protein source for human and animal nutrition from microbes grown on industrial scale. Spirulina (blue-green alga) grown on waste water from potato processing, straw, molasses, animal manure, sewage - produces food rich in protein, minerals, fats, carbohydrates, vitamins. Also reduces environmental pollution. Methylophilus methylotrophus bacterium can produce 25 tonnes of protein due to high biomass production rate. Edible mushrooms are another example of SCP utilization.
nodes.chapter_title: Strategies for Enhancement in Food Production

nodes.label: Origin of Replication (ori)
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Specific DNA sequence in chromosome responsible for initiating replication. Any alien piece of DNA linked to this sequence can replicate within host cells. Controls copy number of linked DNA - for high copy recovery, clone in vector with ori supporting high copy number. Essential feature of cloning vectors. Alien DNA must be linked with ori to multiply in host organism. This linking is the basis of cloning (making multiple identical copies of template DNA).

nodes.label: Genetically Modified Organisms (GMO)
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Plants, bacteria, fungi, and animals whose genes have been altered by manipulation. GM plants have: (1) increased abiotic stress tolerance (cold, drought, salt, heat); (2) reduced reliance on chemical pesticides (pest-resistant crops); (3) reduced post-harvest losses; (4) increased mineral usage efficiency (prevents early soil exhaustion); (5) enhanced nutritional value (e.g., golden rice - Vitamin A enriched). Also used for tailor-made plants supplying starches, fuels, pharmaceuticals to industries.

nodes.label: Bt Cotton
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Cotton with Bt toxin genes incorporated from Bacillus thuringiensis. Specific cry genes used: cryIAc and cryIIAb control cotton bollworms; cryIAb controls corn borer. Most Bt toxins are insect-group specific. Bt toxin kills lepidopterans (tobacco budworm, armyworm), coleopterans (beetles), and dipterans (flies, mosquitoes). Choice of gene depends on crop and targeted pest. Bollgard I and Bollgard II are commercial Bt cotton technologies. Other Bt crops: corn, rice, tomato, potato, soyabean.

nodes.label: Cry Genes and Cry Proteins
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Genes coding for Bt toxin proteins in Bacillus thuringiensis, named 'cry' genes. Multiple types exist with different insect specificities: cryIAc and cryIIAb target cotton bollworms, cryIAb targets corn borer. The proteins form crystals during bacterial growth. These are protoxins (inactive) that become active only in the alkaline pH of insect gut. Insect-group specificity makes them effective bio-pesticides with minimal non-target effects.

nodes.label: RNA Interference (RNAi)
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Method of cellular defense in all eukaryotic organisms involving silencing of specific mRNA by complementary dsRNA molecule that binds to and prevents translation. Used to create pest-resistant plants: nematode Meloidogyne incognita infects tobacco roots. Using Agrobacterium vectors, nematode-specific genes introduced into host plant producing both sense and anti-sense RNA. These form dsRNA initiating RNAi, silencing specific nematode mRNA so parasite cannot survive in transgenic host. Used for gene silencing therapies and cancer treatment research.

nodes.label: Golden Rice
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Genetically modified rice enriched with Vitamin A (beta-carotene). Example of GM crop with enhanced nutritional value. Addresses vitamin A deficiency which is a major health problem in developing countries. Demonstrates how biotechnology can be used for biofortification to improve public health through improved crop nutritional content.

nodes.label: Transgenic Animals
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Animals with DNA manipulated to possess and express extra (foreign) gene. Transgenic rats, rabbits, pigs, sheep, cows, fish produced; 95%+ are mice. Uses: (1) Normal physiology/development study (e.g., insulin-like growth factor); (2) Disease models (cancer, cystic fibrosis, rheumatoid arthritis, Alzheimer's); (3) Biological products - Rosie (1997), first transgenic cow, produced human protein-enriched milk (2.4g/L human alpha-lactalbumin); (4) Vaccine safety testing (transgenic mice for polio vaccine); (5) Chemical/toxicity safety testing.

nodes.label: Rosie - First Transgenic Cow
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: First transgenic cow, produced in 1997. Produced human protein-enriched milk containing 2.4 grams per litre of human alpha-lactalbumin. This milk was nutritionally a more balanced product for human babies than natural cow milk. Demonstrates the use of transgenic animals for producing useful biological products like human proteins.

nodes.label: GEAC (Genetic Engineering Approval Committee)
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Organisation set up by Indian Government to make decisions regarding validity of GM research and safety of introducing GM-organisms for public services. Constituted under the Environment (Protection) Act, 1986 (asked in UPSC 2015). Also known as Genetic Engineering Appraisal Committee. Regulates GM crop approvals in India. Indian law prohibits import of GM food without approval of competent authority.

nodes.label: Biopiracy
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Use of bio-resources by multinational companies and organisations without proper authorisation from countries and people concerned, without compensatory payment. Industrialised nations are financially rich but poor in biodiversity and traditional knowledge; developing world is the reverse. Examples: Basmati rice patent (1997, American company got patent through US Patent Office on variety derived from Indian farmer varieties); attempts to patent turmeric and neem based on Indian traditional herbal medicine. Indian Parliament cleared second amendment of Indian Patents Bill addressing these issues.

nodes.label: Basmati Rice Patent Case
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: In 1997, an American company got patent rights on Basmati rice through US Patent and Trademark Office, allowing sale of a 'new' variety actually derived from Indian farmer varieties (Indian Basmati crossed with semi-dwarf varieties). India has 200,000 rice varieties with 27 documented Basmati varieties grown for centuries with references in ancient texts and folklore. Patent extended to functional equivalents, potentially restricting others selling Basmati. Major example of biopiracy and need for protecting traditional knowledge.

nodes.label: Bioethics and GM Regulation
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Ethical standards required to evaluate morality of human activities that might help or harm living organisms. Genetic modification of organisms can have unpredictable results when introduced into ecosystems. Indian Government set up GEAC for regulating GM research and public services. Growing public anger over companies being granted patents for products using genetic materials long used by farmers and indigenous people. Need for laws to prevent unauthorised exploitation of bio-resources and traditional knowledge.

nodes.label: Pest Resistant Plants (RNAi-based)
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Strategy to prevent nematode infestation of tobacco plants using RNA interference. Nematode Meloidogyne incognita infects tobacco roots causing yield reduction. Using Agrobacterium vectors, nematode-specific genes introduced into host plant. DNA designed to produce both sense and anti-sense RNA in host cells. These complementary RNAs form dsRNA that initiates RNAi, silencing nematode-specific mRNA. Parasite cannot survive in transgenic host. Host plant protected from parasite.

nodes.label: Neem and Turmeric Patent Cases
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Several attempts made to patent uses, products, and processes based on Indian traditional herbal medicines like turmeric and neem. These represent biopiracy - appropriation of traditional knowledge by foreign entities without proper authorisation or compensation. India has successfully challenged some of these patents. Highlights the need for vigilance and immediate countering of such patent applications to protect traditional knowledge and bio-resources.

nodes.label: Ecosystem Structure
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: An ecosystem is a functional unit of nature where living organisms interact among themselves and with the physical environment. Components: abiotic (water, dissolved substances, soil, solar input, temperature, climate) and biotic (producers/autotrophs, consumers/heterotrophs, decomposers). Structural features include species composition and stratification (vertical distribution of species in layers). Ranges from small pond to entire biosphere. Terrestrial: forest, grassland, desert. Aquatic: pond, lake, wetland, river, estuary.

nodes.label: Productivity (GPP, NPP, Secondary)
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Primary production: amount of biomass/organic matter produced per unit area over time by plants during photosynthesis. Expressed as gm-2yr-1 or kcal m-2yr-1. GPP (Gross Primary Productivity) = total rate of organic matter production. NPP (Net Primary Productivity) = GPP minus respiration losses (R). NPP is biomass available for consumers. Secondary productivity = rate of new organic matter formation by consumers. Global annual NPP: ~170 billion tons dry weight; oceans produce only 55 billion tons despite covering 70% of surface.

nodes.label: Decomposition Process
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Breakdown of complex organic matter (detritus: dead plant remains, fecal matter) into inorganic substances (CO2, water, nutrients) by decomposers (fungi, bacteria). Five steps operating simultaneously: (1) Fragmentation - detritivores like earthworms break detritus into smaller particles; (2) Leaching - water-soluble nutrients go into soil; (3) Catabolism - bacterial/fungal enzymes degrade detritus; (4) Humification - forms humus (dark, colloidal, resistant to microbial action, nutrient reservoir); (5) Mineralization - humus degraded to release inorganic nutrients. Rate faster with nitrogen-rich detritus, slower with lignin/chitin. Warm, moist conditions favour decomposition.

nodes.label: Food Chains and Food Webs
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Grazing Food Chain (GFC): starts from producers. Example: Grass -> Goat -> Man. Detritus Food Chain (DFC): begins with dead organic matter, made up of decomposers (saprotrophs). In aquatic ecosystems, GFC is the major conduit for energy. In terrestrial ecosystems, much larger energy fraction flows through DFC. Food web: natural interconnections of multiple food chains. Omnivores like cockroaches and crows connect GFC and DFC. Trophic levels: producers (1st), herbivores (2nd), primary carnivores (3rd), top carnivores (4th).

nodes.label: 10 Percent Law (Lindeman)
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Only 10% of energy is transferred from one trophic level to the next. This limits the number of trophic levels in a grazing food chain to 4-5. From 1,000,000 J of sunlight: producers fix 10,000 J (1%), primary consumers get 1,000 J, secondary consumers 100 J, tertiary consumers 10 J. Proposed by Raymond Lindeman. This progressive decrease in energy at successive trophic levels is the basis for ecological pyramids.

nodes.label: Ecological Pyramids
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Graphical representation of trophic structure: base = producers, apex = top consumers. Three types: (1) Pyramid of Numbers - generally upright in grassland; can be inverted when a single tree supports many insects. (2) Pyramid of Biomass - upright in terrestrial ecosystems; INVERTED in aquatic (sea) ecosystems because phytoplankton biomass < fish biomass (small organisms reproduce faster). (3) Pyramid of Energy - ALWAYS upright, can NEVER be inverted. Limitations: ignores species at multiple trophic levels, assumes simple food chain, excludes saprophytes.

nodes.label: Pyramid of Numbers
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: In grassland: upright - producers (5,842,000) > primary consumers (708,000) > secondary consumers (354,000) > tertiary consumers (3). In a tree ecosystem: inverted because one large tree supports many insects which support fewer birds. The shape depends on the size relationship between organisms at different trophic levels.

nodes.label: Pyramid of Biomass
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Upright in terrestrial ecosystems: producers have highest biomass (809 kg/m2), decreasing at higher levels (PC: 37, SC: 11, TC: 1.5). INVERTED in ocean/aquatic ecosystems: phytoplankton (small standing crop) supports large standing crop of zooplankton and fish. This inversion occurs because phytoplankton reproduce extremely rapidly despite having low biomass at any given time.

nodes.label: Pyramid of Energy
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Always upright, can never be inverted. Energy decreases at each successive trophic level because some is always lost as heat. Values: producers 10,000 J, PC 1,000 J, SC 100 J, TC 10 J from 1,000,000 J sunlight. Each bar represents energy present at that trophic level per unit area per unit time. This is the most accurate representation of ecosystem energy dynamics.

nodes.label: Ecological Succession
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Gradual, predictable change in species composition of an area over time. Ends in a climax community (near equilibrium with environment). Sere = entire sequence of communities. Seral stages = individual transitional communities. Primary succession: on bare areas where no life existed (bare rock, new lava, new pond) - very slow, takes thousands of years. Secondary succession: in areas where community was destroyed (abandoned farmlands, burned forests) - faster because soil already exists. Both types ultimately converge to mesic conditions.

nodes.label: Primary Succession
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Occurs on newly cooled lava, bare rock, new ponds. Pioneer species on rocks are usually lichens, which secrete acids to dissolve rock and aid soil formation. Succession: lichens -> bryophytes -> higher plants -> stable climax forest. Takes several hundred to several thousand years. In water (hydrarch): phytoplankton -> rooted submerged plants -> floating angiosperms -> free-floating plants -> reed-swamp -> marsh-meadow -> scrub -> forest.

nodes.label: Hydrarch and Xerarch Succession
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Hydrarch succession: occurs in wet/aquatic areas, progresses from hydric (wet) to mesic (medium moisture) conditions. Water body gradually converts to land. Xerarch succession: occurs in dry areas, progresses from xeric (dry) to mesic conditions. Dry habitat gradually becomes mesophytic. Both types converge to mesic climax community. Pioneer species differ: phytoplankton in water, lichens on rock.

nodes.label: Climax Community
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The final, stable community in ecological succession that is in near equilibrium with the environment. Remains stable as long as environment remains unchanged. All succession (whether hydrarch or xerarch) converges to a mesic climax community. Natural or human disturbances (fire, deforestation) can revert a seral stage to an earlier one. Characterized by maximum species diversity and biomass.

nodes.label: Nutrient Cycling (Biogeochemical Cycles)
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Movement of nutrient elements through various ecosystem components. Nutrients are recycled indefinitely (unlike energy which flows unidirectionally). Standing state = amount of nutrients in soil at any time. Two types: (1) Gaseous cycles - reservoir in atmosphere (nitrogen, carbon cycles); (2) Sedimentary cycles - reservoir in Earth's crust (sulphur, phosphorus cycles). Rate of release regulated by soil, moisture, pH, and temperature.

nodes.label: Carbon Cycle
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Gaseous type biogeochemical cycle. Carbon = 49% of dry weight of organisms. 71% of global carbon dissolved in oceans (main reservoir). Atmosphere contains only ~1% of total global carbon. 4 x 10^13 kg carbon fixed annually through photosynthesis. Carbon returns to atmosphere via respiration, decomposition, burning of wood/fossil fuels, volcanic activity. Human activities (deforestation, fossil fuel burning) have significantly increased atmospheric CO2. Fossil fuels are also a carbon reservoir.

nodes.label: Phosphorus Cycle
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Sedimentary type biogeochemical cycle. Natural reservoir: rocks containing phosphates. Phosphorus is a major constituent of biological membranes, nucleic acids, and cellular energy transfer systems. Also needed for shells, bones, and teeth. Released by weathering of rocks, absorbed by plant roots, passed through food chain. Phosphate-solubilising bacteria release phosphorus from dead organisms. Key differences from carbon cycle: no respiratory release to atmosphere, much smaller atmospheric inputs through rainfall, negligible gaseous exchanges.

nodes.label: Ecosystem Services
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Products of ecosystem processes: air/water purification, drought/flood mitigation, nutrient cycling, fertile soil generation, wildlife habitat, biodiversity maintenance, crop pollination, carbon storage, aesthetic/cultural/spiritual values. Robert Constanza estimated value at US $33 trillion/year (nearly twice the global GNP of US $18 trillion). Soil formation accounts for ~50% of total ecosystem service value. Climate regulation and wildlife habitat ~6% each. Recreation and nutrient cycling <10% each.

nodes.label: Detritus Food Chain (DFC)
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Begins with dead organic matter (detritus). Composed of decomposers (saprotrophs) - mainly fungi and bacteria that secrete digestive enzymes to break down dead/waste material. In terrestrial ecosystems, a much larger fraction of energy flows through DFC than GFC. Connected with GFC at some levels: DFC organisms may be prey to GFC animals. Omnivores (cockroaches, crows) bridge the two chains. Unlike GFC, there may be no limit on trophic levels in DFC.

nodes.label: Ecological Diversity
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Diversity at the ecosystem level. India with its deserts, rain forests, mangroves, coral reefs, wetlands, estuaries, and alpine meadows has greater ecosystem diversity than a Scandinavian country like Norway. This level of diversity reflects the variety of habitats and ecological processes across a region.

nodes.label: Latitudinal Gradient in Biodiversity
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Species diversity generally decreases from equator towards poles. Tropics (23.5N to 23.5S) harbour more species than temperate or polar areas. Three hypotheses: (1) Tropics had longer evolutionary time (no glaciations disrupting speciation); (2) Tropical environments are less seasonal, more constant, promoting niche specialisation; (3) More solar energy in tropics = higher productivity = greater diversity. Amazonian rain forest has greatest biodiversity: >40,000 plant species, 3,000 fishes, 1,300 birds, 427 mammals, 1,25,000+ invertebrates.

nodes.label: Species-Area Relationship
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Discovered by Alexander von Humboldt in South American jungles. Species richness increases with explored area but only up to a limit (rectangular hyperbola). On log scale: log S = log C + Z log A (S = species richness, A = area, Z = slope/regression coefficient, C = Y-intercept). Z value ranges: 0.1-0.2 for small regions (remarkably similar across taxa - plants in Britain, birds in California, molluscs in New York). Z value: 0.6-1.2 for large areas (entire continents). For frugivorous birds/mammals in tropical forests across continents, slope = 1.15.

nodes.label: Causes of Biodiversity Loss (Evil Quartet)
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Four major causes called 'The Evil Quartet': (1) Habitat loss and fragmentation - most important cause; tropical rain forests reduced from 14% to 6% of Earth's land surface; Amazon being cleared for soya/cattle. (2) Over-exploitation - Steller's sea cow, passenger pigeon extinct due to overexploitation. (3) Alien species invasions - Nile perch in Lake Victoria caused extinction of 200+ cichlid species; invasive weeds: Parthenium (carrot grass), Lantana, Eichhornia (water hyacinth); African catfish Clarias gariepinus threatens Indian catfishes. (4) Co-extinctions - when host species goes extinct, associated parasites/pollinators also die.

nodes.label: Mass Extinction and Sixth Extinction
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Five mass extinction episodes in 3+ billion year history of life. Current 'Sixth Extinction' differs in rate: 100 to 1,000 times faster than pre-human times. IUCN Red List (2004): 784 species extinct in last 500 years (338 vertebrates, 359 invertebrates, 87 plants). Recent extinctions: dodo (Mauritius), quagga (Africa), thylacine (Australia), Steller's sea cow (Russia), 3 tiger subspecies (Bali, Javan, Caspian). 15,500+ species face extinction threat. Amphibians most vulnerable. 12% birds, 23% mammals, 32% amphibians, 31% gymnosperms threatened.

nodes.label: Arguments for Biodiversity Conservation
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Three categories: (1) Narrowly utilitarian - direct economic benefits: food, fibre, firewood, industrial products, medicines. >25% of drugs derived from plants; 25,000 plant species used in traditional medicine. Bioprospecting explores molecular/genetic/species diversity for economic products. (2) Broadly utilitarian - ecosystem services: Amazon produces 20% of Earth's atmospheric oxygen; pollination services by bees, bumblebees, birds, bats. (3) Ethical - every species has intrinsic value; moral duty to preserve biological legacy for future generations.

nodes.label: Biodiversity Hotspots
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Regions with very high species richness AND high degree of endemism (species confined to that region only), also experiencing accelerated habitat loss. Initially 25, later expanded to 34 hotspots worldwide. Three covering India: Western Ghats and Sri Lanka, Indo-Burma, and Himalaya. All hotspots combined cover less than 2% of Earth's land area but harbour extremely high species numbers. Strict protection could reduce ongoing mass extinctions by almost 30%.

nodes.label: In Situ Conservation
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: On-site conservation: protecting the whole ecosystem to save all its biodiversity. India has 14 biosphere reserves, 90 national parks, and 448 wildlife sanctuaries. Sacred groves are religiously/culturally protected forest tracts found in: Khasi and Jaintia Hills (Meghalaya), Aravalli Hills (Rajasthan), Western Ghat regions (Karnataka, Maharashtra), Sarguja/Chanda/Bastar areas (Madhya Pradesh). Meghalaya's sacred groves are last refuges for many rare and threatened plants.

nodes.label: Ex Situ Conservation
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Off-site conservation: threatened species removed from natural habitat to special settings. Methods: zoological parks, botanical gardens, wildlife safari parks. Advanced methods: cryopreservation of gametes (viable and fertile for long periods), in vitro fertilisation, tissue culture propagation of plants, seed banks for different genetic strains of commercially important plants. Many animals extinct in wild continue to be maintained in zoos.

nodes.label: IUCN Red List
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Published by International Union for Conservation of Nature and Natural Resources. Documents species extinctions and threat levels. IUCN Red List 2004: 784 species extinct in last 500 years. Over 15,500 species worldwide currently face threat of extinction. Over 650 threatened species are from India. Categories include: Extinct, Extinct in Wild, Critically Endangered, Endangered, Vulnerable, Near Threatened, Least Concern. Key tool for prioritizing conservation efforts globally.

nodes.label: Endemism
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Species confined to a particular region and not found anywhere else. High endemism is a key criterion for identifying biodiversity hotspots (along with high species richness and accelerated habitat loss). India's Western Ghats, Himalaya, and Indo-Burma hotspots have high levels of endemism. Island ecosystems typically show higher endemism, which also makes them more vulnerable to extinction from invasive species.

nodes.label: Ecosystem Stability and Species Diversity
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: David Tilman's long-term experiments showed that plots with more species had less year-to-year variation in total biomass and higher productivity. A stable community should show low variation in productivity, be resistant or resilient to disturbances, and resist invasion by alien species. Loss of biodiversity leads to decline in plant production, lowered resistance to environmental perturbations (drought), and increased variability in ecosystem processes.

nodes.label: Mega Diversity Countries
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: There are 12 mega diversity countries in the world. India is one of them despite having only 2.4% of the world's land area, it harbours 8.1% of global species diversity. Nearly 45,000 species of plants and ~90,000 species of animals have been recorded from India. Estimated that over 100,000 plant species and 300,000 animal species remain undiscovered in India, applying May's estimate that only 22% of total species have been recorded.

nodes.label: Catalytic Converter
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Fitted in automobiles to reduce emission of poisonous gases. Contains expensive metals: platinum-palladium and rhodium as catalysts. Functions: converts unburnt hydrocarbons to CO2 and water; converts carbon monoxide and nitric oxide to CO2 and nitrogen gas. Vehicles with catalytic converters must use unleaded petrol because lead inactivates the catalyst. Key technology for vehicular pollution control.

nodes.label: CNG and Delhi Vehicular Pollution
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Delhi had more cars than Gujarat and West Bengal combined; ranked 4th among 41 most polluted cities (1990s). Supreme Court PIL led to conversion of entire public transport fleet to CNG by end of 2002. CNG advantages: burns most efficiently with little unburnt residue, cheaper than petrol/diesel, cannot be siphoned or adulterated. Challenge: laying CNG distribution pipelines. Additional measures: phasing out old vehicles, unleaded petrol, low-sulphur fuels, catalytic converters, Bharat Stage IV norms (equivalent to Euro-IV) applied nationwide since April 2017.

nodes.label: Ahmed Khan and Polyblend
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Ahmed Khan, a plastic sack manufacturer in Bangalore, developed Polyblend - a fine powder of recycled modified plastic mixed with bitumen for road laying. In collaboration with R.V. College of Engineering and Bangalore City Corporation, proved that Polyblend-bitumen blend enhances water repellant properties and increases road life by a factor of three. By 2002, over 40 km of road in Bangalore laid using this technique. Raw material: any plastic film waste. Raised ragpicker payment from Rs. 0.40/kg to Rs. 6/kg.

nodes.label: Greenhouse Effect and Global Warming
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Naturally occurring phenomenon heating Earth's surface and atmosphere. Without it, average temperature would be -18C instead of 15C. Mechanism: ~25% solar radiation reflected by clouds/gases, ~50% heats Earth's surface. Earth re-emits infrared radiation, absorbed by greenhouse gases (CO2, methane, N2O, CFCs). CO2 contributes 60%, methane 20%, CFCs 14%, N2O 6% of greenhouse effect. Past century: 0.6C temperature rise, mostly in last 3 decades. Consequences: El Nino, polar ice melting, Himalayan snow cap melting, sea level rise, coastal submergence.

nodes.label: Animal Migration
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The regular seasonal movement of animals from one place to another, usually to escape harsh weather or for breeding. Many birds migrate thousands of kilometres. Siberian cranes migrate to India during winter. Migration is triggered by changes in day length and temperature.

nodes.label: Camouflage
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The ability of animals to blend with their surroundings to avoid detection by predators or prey. Polar bears are white to blend with snow. Chameleons change colour. Stick insects resemble twigs. Camouflage is a survival adaptation.
nodes.chapter_title: Weather, Climate and Adaptations of Animals to Climate

nodes.label: Hibernation
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: A state of deep sleep that some animals enter during winter to conserve energy when food is scarce. Body temperature drops, heartbeat slows, and breathing rate decreases. Bears, frogs, and some squirrels hibernate. It is a survival strategy for cold climates.
nodes.chapter_title: Weather, Climate and Adaptations of Animals to Climate

nodes.label: Air Pressure
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Air exerts pressure in all directions. When air is heated, it expands, becomes lighter, and rises, creating a low-pressure area. Cool air from surrounding high-pressure areas rushes in to fill the gap. This movement of air creates wind.

nodes.label: Wind
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Moving air is called wind. Wind moves from high-pressure areas to low-pressure areas. The greater the difference in pressure, the faster the wind. Wind speed is measured using an anemometer. Wind direction is shown by a wind vane.

nodes.label: Cyclone
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: A very low-pressure system with very high-speed winds revolving around it. Formed over warm ocean waters near the equator. The centre (eye) is calm while surrounding winds are destructive. Called hurricanes in Americas and typhoons in East Asia.

nodes.label: Cyclone Formation
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Warm ocean water heats the air above, which rises rapidly creating very low pressure. Surrounding air rushes in and also gets heated. Due to Earth's rotation, winds start revolving. Continuous supply of moisture and heat intensifies the cyclone.

nodes.label: Thunderstorm
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: A storm accompanied by lightning and thunder, developed from cumulonimbus clouds. Formed when warm, moist air rises rapidly, cools, and condenses. Heavy rain, strong winds, and hail may accompany thunderstorms. Common in hot, humid conditions.

nodes.label: Cyclone Safety Measures
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Safety measures include: moving to safe shelters, staying away from the seashore, storing food and water, not venturing into floodwater, listening to weather forecasts. India has developed effective cyclone warning systems that have reduced casualties.

nodes.label: Anemometer
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: An instrument used to measure wind speed. It consists of rotating cups that spin faster as wind speed increases. Wind speed data is crucial for weather forecasting, aviation, and cyclone tracking.

nodes.label: Uneven Heating of Earth
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The equator receives more direct sunlight than the poles, causing uneven heating. Land heats and cools faster than water. These differences create wind patterns, monsoons, and cyclones. Uneven heating is the primary driver of global wind systems.

nodes.label: Eye of the Cyclone
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The centre of a cyclone where conditions are calm, with clear skies and light winds. It is surrounded by the eyewall, which has the most intense winds and heaviest rainfall. The eye can be 10-30 km in diameter.

nodes.label: India's Cyclone-Prone Coast
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The eastern coast of India (Bay of Bengal) is more vulnerable to cyclones than the western coast. Odisha, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, and West Bengal are frequently affected. The 1999 Odisha super cyclone caused massive devastation.

nodes.label: Sexual Reproduction in Plants
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Reproduction involving seeds, formed by the fusion of male and female gametes. Flowers are the reproductive organs. Involves pollination (transfer of pollen) and fertilisation (fusion of male and female cells). Results in seed and fruit formation.

nodes.label: Budding
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: An asexual reproduction method where a small bulb-like projection (bud) grows from the parent organism, eventually detaching as an independent individual. Seen in yeast and some plants. The bud is genetically identical to the parent.

nodes.label: Fragmentation
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: An asexual reproduction method where the organism breaks into two or more fragments, each growing into a new individual. Seen in algae like Spirogyra. When sufficient nutrients are available, algae grow and break into fragments.

nodes.label: Spore Formation
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: An asexual reproduction method where organisms produce tiny, resistant spores inside spore cases. Spores are dispersed by air, water, or animals. Each spore can grow into a new organism. Seen in fungi (bread mould), ferns, and mosses.

nodes.label: Pollination
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the stigma of a flower. Self-pollination occurs within the same flower. Cross-pollination occurs between different flowers, carried by wind, water, insects, or birds. Cross-pollination promotes genetic variation.

nodes.label: Fertilisation in Plants
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The fusion of male gamete (from pollen tube) with female gamete (egg cell in ovule) to form a zygote. The zygote develops into an embryo within the seed. The ovary develops into a fruit. The ovule becomes the seed.

nodes.label: Seed Dispersal
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The spreading of seeds away from the parent plant to avoid competition. Methods: wind dispersal (dandelion, maple -- light/winged seeds), water (coconut), animals (fruits eaten by birds), explosion (pea pods burst). Ensures species survival over wider areas.

nodes.label: Pollinating Agents
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Agents that transfer pollen between flowers. Insects (bees, butterflies) are attracted by bright petals, nectar, and fragrance. Wind pollinates grasses and many trees. Water pollinates some aquatic plants. Each agent has co-evolved with specific plants.

nodes.label: Fruit and Seed Formation
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: After fertilisation, the ovary develops into a fruit and ovules develop into seeds. The seed contains the embryo (future plant), stored food, and a protective seed coat. Fruits protect seeds and aid in their dispersal.

nodes.label: Pollen Grain
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: A powdery substance produced in the anther of a flower containing male gametes. Each pollen grain can grow a pollen tube through the style to reach the ovule for fertilisation. Pollen is lightweight for easy dispersal.

nodes.label: Unisexual and Bisexual Flowers
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Bisexual (hermaphrodite) flowers have both stamens and pistil (e.g., mustard, rose). Unisexual flowers have either stamens or pistil (e.g., papaya, watermelon). Some plants like maize have both male and female flowers on the same plant.

nodes.label: Water Conservation
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Methods to use water wisely and reduce wastage. Includes fixing leaky taps, using bucket instead of hose for washing, drip irrigation in agriculture, recycling water, and reducing water pollution. Every individual's participation is essential.

nodes.label: Drip Irrigation
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: A water-efficient irrigation method where water is delivered directly to the root zone of plants through a network of pipes with small holes. Reduces water wastage by 50-70% compared to flood irrigation. Widely promoted in water-scarce regions.

nodes.label: World Water Day (March 22)
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Observed on March 22 each year to highlight the importance of freshwater conservation. The UN General Assembly designated this day in 1993. The period 2005-2015 was declared the International Decade for Action 'Water for Life'.

nodes.label: Water Management
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The systematic planning and use of water resources to meet current and future needs. Includes reducing demand, preventing pollution, rainwater harvesting, groundwater recharge, and equitable distribution. Critical for sustainable development.

nodes.label: Forest Ecosystem
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Forests are a complex ecosystem of plants, animals, microorganisms, soil, water, and air interacting together. They have multiple layers: canopy (tall trees), understorey (shorter trees, shrubs), herb layer, and forest floor. Each layer supports different organisms.

nodes.label: Forest Canopy
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The uppermost layer of a forest formed by the branches and leaves of tall trees. The canopy receives the most sunlight. Different trees have different crown shapes. The canopy provides habitat for birds, insects, and epiphytes.

nodes.label: Forest Understorey
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The layer of vegetation beneath the canopy, consisting of shorter trees, shrubs, herbs, and grasses. It receives less sunlight than the canopy. Many shade-loving plants and animals thrive here. Creepers and climbers connect the understorey to the canopy.

nodes.label: Food Chain in Forest
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The chain of feeding relationships: plants (producers) -> herbivores (primary consumers) -> carnivores (secondary consumers) -> top predators. Multiple food chains interlink to form a food web. Each organism depends on others for survival.

nodes.label: Forests and Oxygen
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Forests are called the 'lungs of the Earth' as they produce oxygen through photosynthesis and absorb carbon dioxide. A single large tree can provide oxygen for several people. Forests are the largest terrestrial carbon sinks.

nodes.label: Forests and Water Cycle
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Forests play a crucial role in the water cycle. Tree roots absorb groundwater and release water vapour through transpiration, contributing to cloud formation and rainfall. Forests also prevent soil erosion and help in groundwater recharge.

nodes.label: Forests Prevent Floods and Drought
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Forest canopy and roots slow down rainwater, allowing it to seep into the ground. This recharges groundwater, reduces surface runoff, and prevents floods. In their absence, rainwater rushes directly into rivers, causing floods in rainy season and droughts later.

nodes.label: Impact of Deforestation
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Clearing forests leads to soil erosion, loss of biodiversity, climate change (increased CO2), reduced rainfall, desertification, floods, and droughts. Many animal and plant species face extinction. Deforestation is a major environmental crisis globally.

nodes.label: Forest Products
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Forests provide timber, fuel wood, paper, gum, oils, spices, fodder, and medicinal plants. Minor forest produce (MFP) like honey, lac, bamboo, and tendu leaves are vital for tribal livelihoods. Both timber and non-timber products have economic value.

nodes.label: Seed Dispersal and Regeneration
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Forest floor provides conditions for seeds to germinate and grow into seedlings. Seeds are dispersed by wind, water, animals, and birds. Animals that eat fruits disperse seeds through droppings. This natural regeneration maintains forest cover.

nodes.label: Forest Biodiversity
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Forests harbour an enormous variety of plants, animals, insects, and microorganisms. Different forest types (tropical, temperate, coniferous) support different species. India is a mega-biodiversity country with diverse forest ecosystems.

nodes.label: Crop
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Plants of the same kind cultivated at one place on a large scale for food and economic purposes. India's diverse climatic conditions support a rich variety of crops classified primarily by the season in which they grow.

nodes.label: Kharif Crops
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Crops sown in the rainy season, generally from June to September in India. Major examples include paddy, maize, soyabean, groundnut, and cotton. These crops require substantial water and warm conditions for growth.

nodes.label: Rabi Crops
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Crops grown in the winter season from October to March. Examples include wheat, gram, pea, mustard, and linseed. These crops require cooler temperatures and less water compared to kharif crops.

nodes.label: Irrigation
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The supply of water to crops at regular intervals. Sources include wells, tubewells, ponds, lakes, rivers, dams, and canals. Traditional methods like moat, chain pump, dhekli, and rahat have largely been supplemented by modern techniques.

nodes.label: Sprinkler System
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: An irrigation method where water is sprayed through rotating nozzles on perpendicular pipes joined to a main pipeline. Useful on uneven land and for crops like coffee plantations and lawns where uniform water distribution is needed.

nodes.label: Manure
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: An organic substance obtained from the decomposition of plant or animal wastes by microorganisms. It enhances soil water-holding capacity, makes soil porous, increases friendly microbes, and improves soil texture. Considered better than chemical fertilisers for long-term soil health.

nodes.label: Fertiliser
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Man-made inorganic chemicals rich in specific nutrients like nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium (NPK). Examples include urea, ammonium sulphate, and super phosphate. While they boost crop yield, excessive use reduces soil fertility and causes water pollution.

nodes.label: Crop Rotation
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The practice of growing different crops alternately in the same field to replenish soil nutrients naturally. Growing legumes followed by wheat replenishes nitrogen through Rhizobium bacteria in root nodules of leguminous plants.

nodes.label: Weeding
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The removal of unwanted plants (weeds) that compete with crop plants for water, nutrients, space, and light. Done manually using khurpi or chemically using weedicides like 2,4-D. Best performed before weeds produce flowers and seeds.

nodes.label: Agricultural Practices
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The systematic sequence of farming activities: preparation of soil (tilling/ploughing), sowing, adding manure and fertilisers, irrigation, protecting from weeds, harvesting, and storage. These practices evolved from traditional to modern methods over millennia since 10,000 BCE.

nodes.label: Exhaustible Natural Resources
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Natural resources present in limited quantity that can be exhausted by human activities. Examples include forests, wildlife, minerals, coal, petroleum, and natural gas. Known reserves of fossil fuels will last only a few hundred years, making judicious use essential.

nodes.label: Inexhaustible Natural Resources
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Resources present in unlimited quantity in nature that are not likely to be exhausted by human activities. Examples include sunlight and air. These contrast with exhaustible resources and form the basis for sustainable and renewable energy solutions.

nodes.label: Flora and Fauna
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Flora refers to plants and fauna refers to animals found in a particular area. In Pachmarhi Biosphere Reserve, flora includes sal, teak, mango, jamun, silver ferns, and arjun, while fauna includes chinkara, blue-bull, barking deer, cheetal, leopard, wild dog, and wolf.

nodes.label: Desertification
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The process by which fertile land gradually converts into desert due to deforestation. Removal of the top soil layer exposes lower, hard, rocky layers with less humus and fertility. Reduced vegetation leads to decreased water-holding capacity of soil and altered soil properties.

nodes.label: Fertilisation
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The fusion of a sperm and an ovum, during which their nuclei fuse to form a single nucleus, resulting in a fertilised egg or zygote. This is the first step in sexual reproduction and the beginning of a new individual.

nodes.label: Internal Fertilisation
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Fertilisation that takes place inside the female body. Occurs in many animals including humans, cows, dogs, and hens. Sperms are deposited inside the female body where they meet the egg for fusion.

nodes.label: External Fertilisation
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Fertilisation in which fusion of male and female gametes takes place outside the female body, typically in water. Common in aquatic animals like fish, frogs, and starfish. These organisms produce hundreds of eggs because many are lost to predation and environmental factors.

nodes.label: Viviparous Animals
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Animals that give birth to live young ones rather than laying eggs. Examples include humans, cows, dogs, and cats. The embryo develops inside the mother's body (uterus) receiving nourishment directly from the mother.

nodes.label: Oviparous Animals
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Animals that lay eggs which later develop into young ones. Examples include hens, frogs, lizards, butterflies, and fish. The embryo develops outside the mother's body within the egg, receiving nourishment from the yolk.

nodes.label: Cloning
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The production of an exact copy of a cell or organism. Dolly the sheep, born July 5 1996, was the first cloned mammal, created by Ian Wilmut at the Roslin Institute, Edinburgh. The nucleus from a mammary gland cell was transferred into an enucleated egg. Dolly died on February 14, 2003.

nodes.label: Puberty
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The period during which adolescents reach sexual maturity and become capable of reproduction. Begins around age 10-12 in girls and slightly later in boys. Marked by the onset of menstruation in girls and development of facial hair in boys, triggered by hormonal changes.

nodes.label: Hormones
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Chemical substances secreted by endocrine glands directly into the bloodstream that control and coordinate body functions. They act as chemical messengers and are produced in very small quantities but have significant effects on growth, development, and reproduction.

nodes.label: Endocrine Glands
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Ductless glands that secrete hormones directly into the blood. Include pituitary (master gland controlling other glands), thyroid (thyroxine for metabolism), adrenals (adrenaline for emergencies), pancreas (insulin for blood sugar), and gonads (sex hormones).

nodes.label: Testosterone
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The male sex hormone produced by the testes. It is responsible for the development of male secondary sexual characteristics during puberty including facial hair, deepening of voice, and increased muscle mass. Controls male reproductive development.

nodes.label: Oestrogen
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The female sex hormone produced by the ovaries. It is responsible for the development of female secondary sexual characteristics during puberty including breast development and wider hips. Controls the menstrual cycle and female reproductive development.

nodes.label: Thyroid Gland
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: An endocrine gland that produces thyroxine hormone, which requires iodine for its synthesis. Thyroxine controls the rate of metabolism. Deficiency of iodine causes goitre (swollen thyroid). Iodised salt is recommended in the diet to prevent this condition.

nodes.label: Secondary Sexual Characters
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Physical features that develop during puberty distinguishing males from females but not directly involved in reproduction. In boys: facial hair, deeper voice, broader shoulders. In girls: breast development, wider hips. These are controlled by sex hormones.

nodes.label: Peptic Ulcers
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Once thought to be caused by stress, peptic ulcers were proven by Barry Marshall and Robin Warren to be caused by the bacterium Helicobacter pylori. They received the Nobel Prize in 2005 for this discovery, demonstrating the infectious nature of what was considered a lifestyle disease.

nodes.label: Oxygen Cycle
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: Maintains atmospheric oxygen at 21%. Oxygen is consumed in combustion, respiration, and formation of nitrogen oxides. Returned to atmosphere only through photosynthesis. Also found in Earth's crust as oxides of metals and silicon, and in biological molecules like carbohydrates and proteins.

nodes.label: Biogeochemical Cycles
nodes.subject: science
nodes.detail: The cyclic movement of nutrients through biological, geological, and chemical processes. Water, carbon, nitrogen, and oxygen are continuously recycled. These cycles maintain a balance between various components of the biosphere. Human activities are disrupting these natural cycles.
